metadata.title: AI Text Detection Patterns and Signals for English Language Writing
metadata.description: Comprehensive collection of patterns, statistical signals, linguistic features, and indicators used by various AI-generated text detection tools (commercial, open-source, academic) to identify LLM-written English text. Based on extensive search across arXiv, Hugging Face, GitHub, Wikipedia, and web resources on detectors.
sources_searched: arXiv papers (Kirchenbauer 2023, Mitchell DetectGPT 2023, Wu survey 2023/2025, Fast-DetectGPT, recent 2026 evals)
Commercial tools docs and analyses (GPTZero, Originality.ai, Turnitin, etc.)
metadata.self_review_notes: Covered main statistical (perplexity, burstiness, curvature), visual/forensic (GLTR colors), watermark-specific, stylometric/linguistic, and ML embedding-based patterns. Reviewed for completeness: yes, all major categories from surveys included. Classified separately for clarity. No premature stop; iterated searches until key papers and patterns exhausted.

patterns.description: AI-generated text typically exhibits lower perplexity because LLMs select tokens with high conditional probability, making the text more predictable and 'fluent' in a statistical sense. Human writing tends to have higher perplexity due to more creative, surprising, or varied word choices.
patterns.how_detected: Compute perplexity using a reference language model (e.g., GPT-2, Llama). Lower scores indicate higher likelihood of AI origin. Often combined with thresholds or fed into ML classifiers.
patterns.ai_vs_human: AI: low PPL (e.g. < 10-20 depending on model/domain). Human: higher and more variable.
patterns.limitations_challenges: Sensitive to sampling temperature (higher temp increases PPL), domain (technical text lower PPL), paraphrasing attacks, newer instruction-tuned LLMs can mimic higher PPL. Not sufficient alone for high accuracy.
references: Pangram blog on why PPL/burstiness fail alone

patterns.description: Burstiness measures variation in perplexity, sentence length, or complexity across the text. AI text tends to have lower burstiness (more uniform 'smooth' writing style). Human writing shows 'bursts' of complex/long sentences mixed with simple ones, reflecting natural thought processes.
patterns.how_detected: Calculate variance or standard deviation of per-sentence perplexity or length metrics. Plot or statistical test for uniformity.
patterns.ai_vs_human: AI: low burstiness (consistent style). Human: high burstiness (varied rhythm).
patterns.limitations_challenges: Can be mimicked by prompting LLMs for varied style. Less effective on short texts or highly structured genres (e.g. legal, academic abstracts). Paraphrasing can alter it.
references: Analyses why it fails in isolation (2025 blogs)

patterns.pattern_name: High Proportion of 'Green' Tokens in GLTR Visualization or Similar Forensic Tools
patterns.description: GLTR (Giant Language Model Test Room) colors each token based on its rank in the top predictions of a reference LM (usually GPT-2): Green = top 10 most likely (highly predictable), Yellow = top 100, Red = top 1000, Purple = beyond. AI text shows significantly higher percentage of green tokens because LLMs favor high-probability choices.
patterns.how_detected: Run text through GLTR demo or reimplement; compute % green tokens or statistical test on color distribution. More green = stronger AI signal.
patterns.ai_vs_human: AI-generated: often 50-80%+ green. Human: more balanced mix, higher purple/red (unexpected words).
detectors_using_it: Academic papers extending GLTR (e.g. 2025 arXiv on GLTR-based classification for EN/ES)
Some forensic or educational tools inspired by it
patterns.limitations_challenges: Reference model dependent (GPT-2 old); newer LLMs may differ. Visual interpretation subjective; automated % green needs calibration per domain. Can be evaded by diverse sampling.
references: arXiv:2502.12064 'AI-generated Text Detection with a GLTR-based Approach'

patterns.pattern_name: Elevated Green List Token Ratio + High Z-Score (Watermark Detection)
patterns.description: In LLM watermarking (e.g. Kirchenbauer et al.), during generation the vocab is pseudo-randomly split into 'green list' (boosted) and 'red list' based on hash of previous tokens. Watermarked text has statistically higher fraction of green tokens than expected by chance (~50% for γ=0.5). Detector reproduces the lists and computes z-score on green count.
patterns.how_detected: For a given text, for each position re-compute green/red using same hash/seed from prior token(s), count greens, compute z = (observed_green - expected) / std. High positive z (e.g. >4) indicates watermark with very low FPR.
patterns.ai_vs_human: Watermarked AI: high green ratio + high z-score. Non-watermarked or human: ~50% green, z near 0.
detectors_using_it: Watermark detectors for providers using this scheme (e.g. if OpenAI/Google adopt similar)
Robust to some edits but vulnerable to heavy paraphrasing or tokenization attacks
patterns.limitations_challenges: Only detects if the specific watermark was embedded (not all generators use it; many commercial don't). Private key needed for exact lists in secure mode. Low-entropy text harder to detect. Adversarial editing can reduce z but at quality cost.
references: arXiv:2301.10226 Kirchenbauer et al. 'A Watermark for Large Language Models' - detailed green list algo, z-statistic, robustness theorems

patterns.description: DetectGPT observes that LLM-generated text tends to lie in regions of negative curvature (local 'valleys' or flat areas) in the log-probability function of the model. Human text is more likely in positive curvature areas. By perturbing the text (e.g. with T5) and measuring how log-prob changes, curvature can be estimated without training.
patterns.how_detected: White-box: access to model log-probs. Perturb original text multiple times, compute average curvature or use as feature/score. Fast-DetectGPT optimizes with sampling instead of full perturbations for speed (340x faster, better perf). Black-box variants use surrogate models.
patterns.ai_vs_human: AI-generated: more negative curvature. Human: less or positive.
patterns.limitations_challenges: Requires white-box or good surrogate for best performance. Computationally heavier than simple PPL (though Fast version better). Performance varies by model size/domain; paraphrasing can flatten curvature signals.

patterns.pattern_name: Stylometric and Linguistic Features (Lexical Diversity, Syntactic Patterns, Repetition)
patterns.description: AI text often shows: lower type-token ratio (less lexical diversity), more uniform sentence lengths/structures, higher repetition of phrases or n-grams, preference for certain function words or formal constructions, fewer idioms/colloquialisms/personal anecdotes (depending on prompt), more consistent POS tag distributions or parse tree depths. Humans show more idiosyncratic style, errors, hedging, emotional language.
patterns.how_detected: Feature extraction (avg sentence len var, MTLD or TTR for diversity, n-gram freq stats, readability scores, function word ratios) + traditional ML (SVM, RF, logistic) or as input to transformer classifiers. Some commercial use stylometry + stats.
patterns.ai_vs_human: AI: more formulaic, repetitive, 'safe' formal style, lower diversity in some metrics. Human: higher variance, personal voice, occasional disfluencies.
detectors_using_it: Open-source ML baselines on datasets like HC3, MGTBench
patterns.limitations_challenges: Highly prompt- and domain-dependent (AI can be prompted to be creative/diverse). Easy to evade with good prompting or post-editing. Requires large feature engineering or training data. Cross-generator generalization poor without diverse training.
references: Survey Wu et al. on statistics-based and ML methods

patterns.pattern_name: ML Classifier on Embeddings or Fine-tuned Transformers
patterns.description: Most accurate modern detectors fine-tune transformer models (RoBERTa, DeBERTa, etc.) on large paired datasets of human-written vs AI-generated English text from multiple LLMs/generators. The model learns subtle, distributed patterns in embeddings, attention, token distributions that go beyond simple stats. Some use contrastive learning or hard-negative mining for robustness.
patterns.how_detected: Input text -> tokenizer -> fine-tuned classifier -> probability of 'AI-generated'. Often ensemble with statistical features. HF hosts many such models.
patterns.ai_vs_human: Learns implicit boundary in high-dim space; AI cluster vs human cluster in embedding space for seen generators.
detectors_using_it: Open HF models (e.g. roberta-base-ai-text-detection variants, andreas122001/roberta-mixed-detector)
patterns.limitations_challenges: Overfits to training generators/domains (poor on new LLMs or styles). High false positives on non-native English, translated, or edited text. Requires constant retraining for new models. Black-box nature (no explainability). Data contamination issues.

patterns.pattern_name: Other Signals: Repetition, Formulaic Structures, Lack of Personal Voice or Specific Errors
patterns.description: Additional heuristics: excessive repetition of words/phrases/structures, overuse of transitional phrases ('Furthermore', 'In conclusion'), generic openings, lack of specific personal experiences or idiosyncratic errors typical of humans (typos, inconsistent tense in non-AI), over-use of certain adjectives or formal vocabulary. Some detectors look for 'DNA' like sequences or semantic drift.
patterns.how_detected: Rule-based or feature-based add-ons to ML/stats detectors. N-gram overlap stats, unique n-gram count, semantic consistency checks (entailment models).
patterns.ai_vs_human: AI: more repetitive, templated, 'polished but generic'. Human: unique voice, occasional inconsistencies or creative deviations.
patterns.limitations_challenges: Very prompt-dependent; good prompts reduce formulaicity. Humans in professional writing can be formulaic too (false positives). Weak standalone signal.
references: Analyses of AI writing style in blogs and papers
DNA-GPT and similar specific methods in literature

notes_on_classification_and_coverage: Patterns classified into Statistical, Visual/Forensic, Watermark-specific, Linguistic/Stylometric, ML/Supervised, and Heuristic categories for clarity and to match detector types (some detectors specialize in one, most commercial use ensembles). Self-review: All major patterns from key papers and tools covered. No critical gaps in English text focus. Sources cross-verified via multiple searches.
